q: What does polymorphism mean in OOP?
opts: Hiding the internal details of a class
Binding data with the functions that use it
The ability of the same interface to behave differently for different objects
ansText: The ability of the same interface to behave differently for different objects
expl: Poly = many, morph = forms: one function name or operator works in different ways for different objects (e.g., the same call show() prints different things for different classes).
others: A describes abstraction, B describes inheritance, C describes encapsulation.

q: Which statement best describes procedural programming?
opts: A program is organized as a set of functions that operate on separate data
A program is organized as objects that combine data and functions
A program is written only using classes and inheritance
A program is written without using any functions
ansText: A program is organized as a set of functions that operate on separate data
expl: In procedural programming (like C), data and functions are separate; functions pass data around. OOP instead bundles data + functions together into objects.
others: B, C describe OOP; D is simply wrong - procedural programs do use functions.

q: In a non-static member function, what does the this pointer hold?
opts: The address of the class definition
The address of the object that called the function
The address of the first data member only
The address of the base class
ansText: The address of the object that called the function
expl: this is automatically passed to every non-static member function and always points to the exact object used in the call, e.g. s.display() makes this point to s.
others: A class definition has no address at runtime; this is not limited to one member; it belongs to the actual object's class.

q: Which OOP concept allows a new class to acquire the properties of an existing class?
expl: A derived class automatically gets the data members and member functions of its base class, then can add or override its own.

q: Which OOP concept binds data and the functions that operate on it into a single unit?
expl: A class encapsulates data + the methods that use it in one unit and hides the data from outside - like a capsule.

q: What is the default access specifier for members of a class in C++?
expl: In a C++ class, members written before any access specifier are private. (Note the trap: for a struct the default is public - for a class it is private.)

q: What is an object in C++?
opts: A blueprint that defines data members and member functions
A function that returns a value
expl: The class is the blueprint; each variable created from it (e.g., Box b1;) is an object - a real instance occupying memory.
others: A describes the class itself, not an object.

q: Which operator is used to define a member function outside its class?
expl: Outside definition uses the form  void Box::volume() { ... }  - the :: tells the compiler that volume belongs to class Box.

q: Which keyword is used to define a class in C++?
expl: Syntax: class Box { ... };  - note the semicolon after the closing brace (forgetting it is a classic compile error).

q: Which C++ data type is used to store the values true and false?
expl: bool holds only true (1) or false (0). Printing a bool with cout shows 1 or 0, not the words.

q: Which symbol is used at the start of a destructor's name?
expl: A destructor is written ~Box() with the same name as the class preceded by ~. It runs automatically when the object is destroyed.

q: How many copies of a static data member exist for a class, regardless of how many objects are created?
opts: One copy shared by all objects
ansText: One copy shared by all objects
expl: A static data member belongs to the class, not to any object - every object reads and writes the same single variable (must be defined outside the class, e.g. int Player::highest = 0;).

q: What is the return type of a constructor?
expl: Constructors never declare a return type. Writing void Box() { } makes it NOT a constructor (a trap option in output questions).
